Your reading of the populations is right except where noted; every count below was recomputed from the exported tables and reproduces.
  > 
  > **1. Populations** (all at noise multiple 0.5 unless stated; "a–f" are the six planned mechanisms; (g) is the convex mirror)
  > - **2193** (Table 1, per noise level; 126 runs): s ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 0.75}, mechanisms a–f, Bernoulli *and* cluster designs, every run except the fine-s and p-grid runs. It includes the edge-noise, no-baseline sanity and convex-mirror (c) runs.
  > - **1797** (Bernoulli rows of Table 1; 104 runs): the same, Bernoulli only. 2193 − 1797 = the 396 cluster-design cells.
  > - **2178** (diagnostic cells; 121 runs; Fig. 5 and the absolute R² of log RMSE): s > 0, a–f, both designs (1782 Bernoulli + 396 cluster), edge-noise and sanity runs included. It excludes the 15 convex-mirror cells that Table 1 keeps (hence 2193 − 15).
  > - **1800** (Fig. 4; 94 runs): Bernoulli, true feature graph (no edge noise), a–f, s > 0, fine-s runs included; no sanity, convex-mirror or p-grid runs. It is a subset of 1797 (the 108 edge-noise, 36 sanity and 15 convex cells are out, the 162 fine-s cells in).
  > - **1974** (oracle rule; 107 runs): *every* Bernoulli cell with s > 0, mechanisms a–g, except the p-grid runs. It therefore includes edge-noise, sanity and the convex mirror, including the 15 cells of (g), so "a–f" is wrong for it.
  > - **1440** (ŝ rule; 80 runs): the cells of the 1974 that have an estimated share in the exported table, 240 per mechanism a–f. 36 of them are edge-noise or sanity cells (18 each), a storage artefact. Dropping them changes the rule from 91.8% to 91.95% right on the remaining 1404, and the base rate from 80.2% to 80.3%.
  > - **1224** (exact bias prediction; 68 runs): non-null cells a–f at s ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 0.75} that have the exact population-OLS prediction: 204 per mechanism; families, real graphs, core, size and sanity runs. There is none for cluster, edge-noise, community-baseline or fine-s cells.
  > - **9795** (Fig. A2A; 107 runs): every Bernoulli cell with a mechanism a–f at all five noise multiples (0.25–4) in the Tier G regression, p-grid runs excluded. It is 1959 cells × 5 noise multiples and includes the fine-s grid (s = 0.1…0.9).
  > 
  > **2. Learner parity on (d)** (`parity_d.csv`, 10000 resamples; the median is the median of per-cell ratios of RMSE to the regression, as in the tier summary):
  > 
  > | learner | median ratio | 95% interval (cells) | 95% interval (runs) |
  > |---|---|---|---|
  > | boosting | 0.99 | [0.70, 1.18] | [0.70, 1.18] |
  > | random forest | 1.09 | [0.76, 1.59] | same |
  > | adaptive Hájek | 1.02 | [0.59, 1.73] | same |
  > | lasso | 2.00 | [1.88, 2.56] | same |
  > | ridge | 2.04 | [1.83, 3.42] | same |
  > 
  > Two things for the text. (a) On (d) there are only 14 cells (12 for the adaptive Hájek), one per run, so cell and run resampling give the same interval. (b) These intervals are wide: they include ratios 30% below to 60–70% above 1, and half the cells lie below 1 for each of the three. The evidence is "not distinguishable from the regression", not "matches". **Lasso and ridge do not match on (d): they are about twice the regression's RMSE and their intervals exclude 1.** "On the threshold mechanism (d) they match it" and the abstract's "under the threshold mechanism they match it" therefore hold for three of the five learners only; please name them. On a–c, e, f the median ratio is 1.98–2.80 and every interval is above 1 (e.g. boosting [1.68, 2.23] by cells, [1.44, 2.28] by runs), so "none beats the regression" holds there with interval support; the 1.6–3.8 in the text are per-mechanism medians, which these pooled ones summarise.
  >
